I don't see `LICENSE`, `DISCLAIMER.md`, `SECURITY.md`, or the compliance-boundaries doc in this working directory, so I can't verify the actual disclaimer text against the proposed copy — but the wording itself has a problem independent of that.

**Why I can't sign off:**

"MIT boilerplate elsewhere covers us" and "it's just marketing" don't hold up here, because the two things — *permission to use* and *proof of fitness* — are separate claims, and this sentence collapses them:

- "SOC2-ready" and "compliance-critical" are **compliance claims**. SOC2 is an actual audit standard with a formal report; "ready" implies you've evaluated the toolkit against those controls. If there's no SOC2 report or control mapping backing this, it's an unsupported compliance claim, not marketing flavor.
- "Enterprise-grade" and "battle-tested" are **assurance claims** about robustness/reliability that need evidence (production usage data, test coverage, incident history) — not just confidence.
- "Trusted by teams running regulated workloads" implies **specific customer validation for regulated use**. If you can't name/cite that, it's an unsupported claim, and in a regulated context (SOC2, HIPAA, etc.) that's the kind of line that creates real liability regardless of MIT disclaimers.
- A disclaimer file in the repo root doesn't neutralize this: the boundary wording needs to sit *where users form their expectations* — the README hero and `--help` banner are exactly those places, and right now they say the opposite of the disclaimer.

**Banned phrases in your draft (all currently in an affirmative/promotional sentence, not a disclaimer):** "enterprise-grade," "SOC2-ready," "battle-tested," "compliance-critical," "trusted by ... regulated workloads."

**What to change it to** — replace assurance words with wording tied to evidence anyone can verify (tests, docs, license), and keep the "does not create compliance" line adjacent, not buried in a separate file:

> **README hero:**
> "A fast, well-tested [toolkit description] for [actual use case]. MIT licensed, open source, actively maintained. This tool does not create SOC2, compliance, or regulatory certification for your environment — see DISCLAIMER.md."

> **CLI `--help` banner (short form):**
> "[Tool name] v[X] — MIT licensed. No compliance, certification, or fitness-for-regulated-use claims are made; see DISCLAIMER.md."

If you actually have a SOC2 report, specific test coverage numbers, or named reference customers, you can cite those specifically ("94% test coverage," "SOC2 Type II report available on request," "used in production by [named company]") — specific, checkable claims are fine; vague assurance words are the problem.

**Escalation:** If you want to keep any SOC2/compliance language at all, that needs sign-off from whoever holds your actual SOC2 report/audit, not me — that's a compliance/legal call, not a wording call.
